concept.name: Pairs divergence trade
concept.definition: The entry logic of a pairs trade: positioning as the spread between two linked securities diverges to an extreme, on the expectation that the divergence has run its course and the spread will close. In the Gatev-Goetzmann-Rouwenhorst framework, divergence beyond two historical standard deviations is precisely the event that triggers the dollar-neutral position.
concept.intuition: Divergence is the signal, not the enemy: you wait for the rubber band between two stocks to stretch beyond historical tolerance, then take the position that profits as it snaps back.
concept.mechanics: During the trading period, monitor the normalized-price spread of a formed pair; a divergence beyond +/-2 historical standard deviations opens the dollar-neutral long/short. Risk management defines a maximum adverse divergence (stop), because spreads can widen arbitrarily before closing - or never close.
concept.formula: Trigger: |s_t| > 2 sigma_s, where s is the normalized price spread; position = short the high leg, long the low leg, in equal dollar amounts.
concept.failure_modes: The central risk is divergence that never closes: structural breaks turn the entry signal into a trap, and each unit added to a widening spread increases exposure exactly as the probability of a permanent break rises.
concept.misconceptions: That larger divergence means a better trade; beyond some point, extreme divergence correlates with pair breakdown (for example, an impending acquisition of one leg), so the biggest apparent opportunities carry the highest breakdown risk.
concept.example: A pair's spread widens from 0 to -2.2 sigma over two weeks on no news; the trader buys the lagging leg and shorts the leader, with a stop at -3.5 sigma in case the relationship has broken.

citations.source: Gatev, Goetzmann & Rouwenhorst, 'Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule' (SSRN; published RFS 2006)
